veranderings.voor: Jou arms raak moeg en die sak
veranderings.na: Jou arms raak moeg, en die sak
veranderings.rede: Two clauses each with their own subject and verb are joined by en, so AWS 2017 requires a comma.

veranderings.voor: 'n klein vrag op 'n slag ver neem
veranderings.na: 'n klein vrag op 'n slag ver dra
veranderings.rede: The paragraph is about carrying by hand, and 'ver dra' is more natural and precise than 'ver neem'.

veranderings.blok: Op sy rug of agter hom aan
veranderings.voor: op sy rug. Of hy trek
veranderings.na: op sy rug, of hy trek
veranderings.rede: A sentence opening with 'Of' reads as a fragment; joining the two clauses with a comma before 'of' follows AWS and flows better.

veranderings.voor: wat daar kan leef en werk
veranderings.na: wat daar kon leef en werk
veranderings.rede: The sentence is in the past (het ... gekies), so the relative clause should be past too.
'Die plaas' points to one specific farm that was never introduced; the general statement needs 'plase'.

veranderings.voor: Die vet is 'n stoor van energie
veranderings.rede: 'n stoor van energie' copies English 'a store of energy' and repeats 'gestoor' from the sentence before; 'voorraad' is the idiomatic word and 'energie' is kept.
Afrikaans uses the possessive for a body part here; 'met 'n hand' sounds wooden.

veranderings.voor: swaarder goed dra as wat 'n mens self kan dra
veranderings.na: 'n swaarder vrag dra as wat 'n mens self kon dra
veranderings.rede: 'swaarder goed' is awkward and the comparison should stay in the past tense like the main clause (kon).

veranderings.voor: om vinniger te reis as wat 'n dier stap
veranderings.na: om vinniger te reis as wat 'n dier kon stap
veranderings.rede: The comparison clause needs a modal in the past to match the past-tense sentence; 'as wat 'n dier stap' reads incomplete.

veranderings.voor: net so vinnig gegaan as wat die dier kon gaan
veranderings.na: net so vinnig gegaan as wat die dier kon stap
veranderings.rede: Avoids the clumsy repetition gegaan/gaan and matches 'stap' used for the animals throughout the lesson.
'na hom kyk' can read as 'look at him' (from English 'look after'); 'na hom omsien' clearly means care for him.
